SPXC is still sitting on a passive $205 sell-limit with a $186.90 stop underneath, not an active market exit — that's not the same thing as "exiting." Recommend cancelling the resting $205 limit and exiting at market (or an aggressive marketable limit) today, regardless of price. If this already filled since the last sync and portfolio.json just hasn't been updated, tell portfolio-manager so the record catches up — but don't assume that; act on what's actually on the book.

The exit is on the defense-electronics (Kranze) segment tripping your no-defense rule, not performance. Action implication: see the urgent alert above — cancel the passive bracket and exit at market today.

📚 Today you learned

NBBO (National Best Bid and Offer)

NBBO is the consolidated best bid and best ask across every US exchange at a given instant — the "official" tradeable price, as opposed to whatever any single data feed happens to report. Retail platforms and most secondary sources (Yahoo, Google, a news search) are quoting a snapshot that's already stale by the time it renders; your broker's own quote screen pulls the live NBBO directly. Today is a clean example of why that distinction matters: this report's normal price source (Yahoo Finance JSON API, with a stooq fallback) was completely unreachable from this environment, so every number above that depends on price — P&L, the goal tracker, GOOG's distance to its $333.90 stop — had to be labeled unavailable rather than guessed. The one number I did surface (a ~$335.72 GOOG print from a web search) is not the NBBO — it's someone else's stale snapshot, good enough to flag "check this now," not good enough to act on directly. When your automated feed goes dark, the NBBO in IBKR is always the fallback of record, not a search result.

Also today: Feed redundancy — a single data source (even a good one) is a single point of failure; today's outage is exactly the scenario the "never estimate, never use search for prices" rule in this skill was written for.
